key_insight: Across ClinicalTrials.gov trials, sex reporting was nearly universal, gender reporting was rare, and female participation was generally low relative to disease burden.
clinical_relevance: Incomplete gender reporting and female underrepresentation can limit assessment of how broadly trial findings apply.
method: Cross-sectional analysis of 58,007 interventional trials with posted results.
Assessed reporting associations with funding, location, enrollment, and other trial characteristics.
Compared female trial participation with female disease prevalence using participation-to-prevalence ratios (PPRs) across 10 conditions.
evidence_signal: Sex was reported in 99.44% of trials and gender in 0.95%; 43.0% of 16,097 trial–condition combinations achieved a female PPR of at least 0.90.
watch_item: This observational registry analysis identifies reporting and representation gaps, not their causes; it does not evaluate AI or cancer drug discovery.
paper_title: Sex and Gender Reporting and Female Participation Relative to Disease Burden in ClinicalTrials.gov
